deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (my interpretation). The bundle is Riemann's work on the self-gravitating homogeneous fluid ellipsoid. His 1861 paper is 'Ein Beitrag zu den Untersuchungen über die Bewegung eines gleichartigen flüssigen Ellipsoides'. The integrals are the usual ellipsoidal potential integrals ∫ds/sqrt((a²+s)(b²+s)(c²+s)), in normalized form. Put s -> ab·s and fix the volume, abc=1. Then (a²+s)(b²+s) becomes proportional to 1+2xs+s², with x=(a²+b²)/(2ab)≥1. Also c²+s becomes proportional to 1+s/c³, where the symbol 'c³' stands for c²/(ab)=c³. Throughout the page Δ = sqrt((1+2xs+s²)(1+s/c³)). This is confirmed by Riemann's own derivatives of u=∫ds/Δ further down.

(1) Definition and first rewriting.
- p = ∫_0^∞ (ds/Δ)[(s+1)/(1+2xs+s²) − c³/(c³+s)].
- Since −c³/(c³+s) = −1 + s/(c³+s), the integrand becomes ((1−2x)s − s²)/(1+2xs+s²) + s/(c³+s). This is correct.

(2) Integration by parts of the last term.
- d(1+s/c³)^{-1/2} = −(1/2)(1+s/c³)^{-1/2} ds/(c³+s).
- Hence (ds/Δ)·s/(c³+s) = −2(1+2xs+s²)^{-1/2} s d(1+s/c³)^{-1/2}.
- This equals +2∫(1+s/c³)^{-1/2} d[s(1+2xs+s²)^{-1/2}].
- The boundary term vanishes at 0 and at ∞; it behaves like s^{-1/2}. Riemann leaves this implicit.
- With d/ds[s(1+2xs+s²)^{-1/2}] = [(1+2xs+s²) − (x+s)s]/(1+2xs+s²)^{3/2}, the numerator is 2(1+2xs+s²) − 2(x+s)s + (1−2x)s − s² = 2+s−s².
- So p = ∫_0^∞ (ds/Δ)(2+s−s²)/(1+2xs+s²). This is correct.

(3) Symmetric form.
- Use 1+2xs+s² = s(s+1/s+2x) and 2+s−s² = (2−s)(1+s).
- Then p = ∫_0^∞ (s+1/s+2x)^{-3/2} dlog s (s^{-1/2}+s^{1/2}) (2−s)/sqrt(1+s/c³). This is correct.
- Split the range at s=1 and map s→1/s on [1,∞). The factors (s+1/s+2x) and (s^{-1/2}+s^{1/2}) are invariant.
- So p = ∫_0^1 (…)^{-3/2} dlog s (s^{-1/2}+s^{1/2}) [(2−s)/A + (2−1/s)/B], with A = sqrt(1+s/c³) and B = sqrt(1+1/(c³s)).
- Riemann factors the bracket using s = c³(A²−1) and 1/s = c³(B²−1).
- The correct factorization is (2−s)/A + (2−1/s)/B = c³(1/A+1/B)(1 + 2/c³ − AB).
- He then rationalizes 'k − AB' with k=2+1/c³, writing k² − A²B² = 3 + 4/c³ − (s+1/s)/c³. Note A²B² = 1 + (s+1/s)/c³ + 1/c⁶.
- This line of attack, presumably meant to decide the sign of p, is then abandoned.

(4) Target expression (presumably the stability/characteristic condition).
- Read as: 2μ⁴(1+2xc³) + μ²·2[(1+x)p + (1−x)q] − [(1+x)∂p/∂log c + (1−x)∂q/∂log c] + 2q(1+2c³)(1+x) + 2p(1−2c³)(1−x) + [(1+2c³)∂q/∂x − (1−2c³)∂p/∂x](x²−1).
- Here q = ∫_0^∞ (ds/Δ)(−2+s+s²)/(1+2xs+s²), the companion of p.
- Riemann forms combinations, dropping the common denominator 1+2xs+s² in writing:
  - (1+x)p + (1−x)q ↔ 2s + 2x(2−s²).
  - (1+2c³)q + (2c³−1)p ↔ 4c³s − 2(2−s²).
  - 2(p+q)(1+2c³x) − 2(p−q)(x+2c³) ↔ 4s(1+2c³x) − 4(2−s²)(x+2c³).
  - These use p+q ↔ 2s and p−q ↔ 2(2−s²).
- All are correct once the denominator is restored.

(5) Derivatives via u = ∫(1+2xs+s²)^{-1/2}(1+s/c³)^{-1/2} ds.
- ∂u/∂log c = (3/2)∫(ds/Δ) s/(s+c³) = (3/2)∫(ds/Δ³)(s/c³)(1+2xs+s²).
- ∂u/∂x = −∫(ds/Δ³) s(1+s/c³).
- ∂²u/∂x∂log c = −(3/2)∫(ds/Δ³) s²/c³.
- All three are correct.
- He then reduces everything to integrals with Δ³ in the denominator, with polynomial numerators.
- Key result: p = ∫(ds/Δ³) s[(1+1/c³−2x) + s(1/c³−1)].
  - This follows (implicit step, mine) from p = ∫(ds/Δ³)(2+s−s²)(1+s/c³).
  - One then subtracts the exact derivative Δ³·d/ds(2s/Δ) = 2 + s(2x+1/c³) − s³/c³, whose integral over (0,∞) is 0. I verified this.
- ∂p/∂log c = ∫(ds/Δ³)(3/2)(s/c³)(2+s−s²). This is correct.
- (x+1)∂p/∂x is claimed to equal ∫(ds/Δ³)·(−1/2)(s/c³)[s² + s(2x − 2x/c³ + 3/c³) − 4xc³]. I did not verify this claim.

(6) Assembly.
- He assembles 2p(1−2c³) − (x+1)∂p/∂log c − (x+1)(x+2c³)∂p/∂x into a single integrand of the form (s/(2c³))·B(s)/Δ³.
- B = [(x+2c³) + 3(x+1)]s² + s[k(x+2c³) − 3(x+1) + 2(1/c³−1)(1−2c³)] − 4xc³(x+2c³) − 6(x+1) + 2(1−2c³)(1+1/c³−2x), with k = 2x − 2x/c³ + 3/c³.
- He then expands the s-coefficient and starts factoring, apparently to find the sign or roots of the polynomial. The page ends mid-computation.
errors: In the symmetrization step the factor should be (1 + 2/c³ − AB), since (1/c³)·[(2−s)/A+(2−1/s)/B] = (1/A+1/B)(1+2/c³−AB). Riemann writes (2 + 1/c³ − AB) and rationalizes with (2+1/c³)², so the subsequent line '3+4/c³−(s+1/s)/c³' inherits the slip. The correct value of (1+2/c³)²−A²B² is (4+3/c³−(s+1/s))/c³. The route is abandoned, so it has no consequence.
The combinations (1+x)p+(1−x)q etc. are written without the common denominator 1+2xs+s². They are correct only with that denominator understood.
Integration by parts: the vanishing of the boundary terms at 0 and ∞ is not stated (it is true). In the passage from the Δ-form to the Δ³-form of p, the exact derivative d(2s/Δ) is dropped silently.

In the assembled polynomial B, the contribution of the 2p(1−2c³) term appears with coefficient 2(1−2c³)(…). Using p=∫(ds/Δ³)s[…] and the overall prefactor s/(2c³), it should be 4c³(1−2c³)(…). This is either a factor-2c³ slip or a different normalization of that term; the reading is uncertain.

Expansion of the s-coefficient: my computation gives (1/c³)(2+3x−2x²) + 4c³(x+1) + 2x² − 7x − 3. The page shows (as transcribed) 4c³(x−1) and '+4x²−7x−2'. This is either a slip or a transcription problem.
The claimed formula for (x+1)∂p/∂x was not verified here.

results.what: Reduction of the ellipsoidal potential combination p to ∫ds/Δ·(2+s−s²)/(1+2xs+s²) by integration by parts, with Δ²=(1+2xs+s²)(1+s/c³) (normalized axes, abc=1)
results.modern_name: Manipulation of index-symbol / elliptic integrals for homogeneous ellipsoids (Chandrasekhar's A_i, A_ij integrals)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard since Dirichlet, Dedekind, Riemann (1860-61); systematized by Chandrasekhar (1960s)

results.what: Symmetrization of the integral under s→1/s on [1,∞) to an integral over [0,1]
results.modern_name: Inversion symmetry of the integrand (Landen-type / s↔1/s folding)

results.what: Expression of p, ∂p/∂log c, ∂p/∂x as ∫ds/Δ³ times polynomials, via derivatives of u=∫ds/Δ and the exact differential d(2s/Δ)
results.modern_name: Reduction of elliptic integrals by differentiation under the integral sign / integration by parts (recurrence relations of index symbols)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Legendre, Jacobi); for ellipsoids, Chandrasekhar's recurrence relations

results.what: Assembly of a (presumed) stability/characteristic expression in μ with coefficients built from p, q and their x- and c-derivatives
results.modern_name: Stability analysis of Riemann ellipsoids (second-order virial / energy criterion)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1861 (energy criterion); corrected and extended by Lebovitz (1966) and Chandrasekhar (1965-69)

deep.surprise_reason: Working computations toward the published 1861 ellipsoid paper (equilibrium/stability integrals in normalized variables). The methods are routine integral manipulations. Riemann's stability analysis of fluid ellipsoids is already known and credited to him; nothing here goes beyond it.

checkable.asserts: First rewriting of the integrand of p (should be 0).
Numerator after integration by parts equals 2+s-s^2 (should be 0).
Derivative used in the integration by parts (should be 0).
Correct symmetrized factor is (1+2/c3 - AB), not (2+1/c3 - AB) (should be 0).
Integrand of p over Delta^3 differs from Riemann's s[(1+1/c3-2x)+s(1/c3-1)] by an exact derivative with zero integral (should be 0).
Integrand of d^2u/dx dlog c = -(3/2)s^2/c^3/Delta^3 (should be 0).
Numerical test (at x=1.3, c=1.1) of the claimed formula for (x+1)dp/dx; unverified claim on the page. Note x+1 = 2.3 must multiply the finite-difference derivative.
s-coefficient of B; should equal (2+3x-2x^2)/c3 + 4c3(x+1) + 2x^2 - 7x - 3, to compare with the page's '4c^3(x-1)' and '+4x^2-7x-2'.

transcription_corrections: '(x+x)' in the long μ-expression is almost certainly '(1+x)'.
'μ(2(...)p+(1−x)q)' is probably μ²·2[(1+x)p+(1−x)q] (exponent of μ uncertain).
In the integration-by-parts line, 's^{1/2}' should read 's' (the factor is s(1+2xs+s²)^{-1/2}), consistent with the RHS d((1+2xs+s²)^{-1/2}s).
In the symmetrized integral the transcribed factor '2+1/c³' matches Riemann's subsequent rationalization (4+4/c³+1/c⁶), so it is likely what he wrote; mathematically it should be 1+2/c³.
The '1' under '4c³s−2(2−s²)' and the missing denominators in the p,q combinations stand for the omitted common denominator 1+2xs+s².
'4c³(x−1)' and '−1−4' in the expansion line may be misreadings (the correct expansion gives 4c³(x+1) and −6 from 2(1/c³−1)(1−2c³)).
